title: Sinigang na baboy
intro: Pork ribs simmered until tender in a broth soured with fresh tamarind, loaded with radish, long beans, eggplant, okra and water spinach. Sharp, savory and best with plenty of rice.

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Rinse the pork, put it in a large pot with the 2 liters of water and bring to a boil. Skim off the gray foam as it rises.
Add the onion and tomatoes, lower the heat, cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
While the broth simmers, boil the tamarind in the 2 cups of water until the skins split and the flesh turns soft.
Mash the tamarind in its water with a fork, then press it through a strainer into a bowl. Discard the seeds and skins and keep the thick sour juice.
Add the radish to the pot and simmer until it starts to turn translucent.
Add the long beans, eggplant and okra and simmer until just tender.
Stir in half of the tamarind juice, the chilies and the fish sauce. Taste and add more tamarind juice until it is as sour as you like.
Turn off the heat, push the water spinach into the hot broth, cover and let it wilt.
Serve hot with steamed rice and a small dish of fish sauce with crushed chili on the side.

tips: No fresh tamarind? A 40 g pack of tamarind soup base works for this amount. Add half, taste, then add more.

title: Sinigang na liempo
intro: Pork belly sinigang with taro cooked until it falls apart and thickens the broth, made the weeknight way with a packet of tamarind soup base. Rich, sour and slightly creamy.

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Put the pork belly and water in a pot and bring to a boil. Skim off the foam.
Add the onion and tomatoes, cover and simmer over low heat until the pork is tender.
Add the taro and simmer until it is very soft and starting to fall apart.
Mash a few pieces of taro against the side of the pot so they dissolve and thicken the broth.
Add the radish and simmer until it turns translucent.
Add the okra and simmer until bright green and tender.
Stir in the tamarind soup base a little at a time, tasting as you go. Add the chilies and season with fish sauce.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until it wilts. Serve hot.

tips: Soup base brands differ in strength and saltiness, so add the fish sauce only after the soup base is in.

title: Sinigang na baboy sa bayabas
intro: Pork sinigang soured with ripe guavas, which give the broth a gentle, fruity sourness and a fragrant aroma. Milder and sweeter than tamarind sinigang.

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Bring the pork and water to a boil in a large pot and skim off the foam.
Add the onion and tomatoes, cover and simmer over low heat until the pork is nearly tender.
Add the guavas and taro and simmer until the guavas are very soft.
Scoop the guavas into a strainer set over a bowl. Mash them through with the back of a spoon, scraping the pulp from underneath, and stir the pulp back into the pot. Discard the seeds and skins.
Add the long beans and simmer until tender.
Add the chilies and season with fish sauce. Taste: the broth should be mildly sour and sweet.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach, cover and let it wilt.
Serve hot with rice.

tips: Slightly underripe guavas give more sourness, very ripe ones more fragrance. A mix of both is ideal.

title: Sinigang na baboy sa kamias
intro: Pork ribs simmered with fresh kamias, the small green fruit that melts into the broth and gives it a bright, puckery sourness. A favorite in homes with a kamias tree in the yard.

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Bring the pork and water to a boil and skim off the foam.
Add the onion and tomatoes, cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the kamias and simmer until they turn olive green and soften completely.
Press about half the kamias against the side of the pot with a ladle so they break down into the broth.
Add the radish and simmer until it starts to turn translucent.
Add the eggplant and long beans and simmer until just tender.
Add the chilies and season with fish sauce. If it is not sour enough, simmer a few more kamias in the broth.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve hot.

tips: Kamias sourness varies a lot from tree to tree. Start with 15 and keep a few more on hand.

title: Sinigang na baboy sa santol
intro: Pork sinigang soured with santol, the fuzzy summer fruit whose flesh cooks down into a sour, slightly sweet and gently astringent broth.

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Bring the pork and water to a boil and skim off the foam.
Add the onion and tomatoes, cover and simmer until the pork is nearly tender.
Add the santol and taro and simmer until the santol is soft enough to mash.
Scoop out the santol, mash it through a strainer into the pot and discard the fibers that stay behind.
Simmer a few more minutes so the santol pulp blends into the broth.
Add the long beans and simmer until tender.
Add the chilies and season with fish sauce, tasting for a good balance of sour and salty.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve hot.

tips: Firm, slightly underripe santol is the most sour. If yours are sweet, add a little tamarind juice to sharpen the broth.

title: Sinigang na baboy sa pakwan
intro: Pork sinigang with watermelon cooked into the broth, which turns it rosy and adds a light sweetness that rounds out the tamarind sourness.

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Bring the pork and water to a boil and skim off the foam.
Add the onion and tomatoes, cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Blend or mash 2 cups of the watermelon and pour the juice into the pot through a strainer.
Add the radish and simmer until it starts to turn translucent.
Add the long beans and the remaining watermelon cubes and simmer until the beans are tender.
Stir in the tamarind soup base a little at a time until the broth is sour with a sweet finish. Add the chilies and season with fish sauce.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve hot.

tips: Add the watermelon cubes near the end so they hold their shape. Cooked too long, they turn mushy.

title: Sinigang na baboy sa mangga
intro: Pork ribs simmered with slices of hard green mango, which soften into the broth and give it a fresh, tangy sourness with a hint of mango aroma.

items.name: medium green (unripe) mangoes
items.note: peeled and sliced off the seed

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Bring the pork and water to a boil and skim off the foam.
Add the onion and tomatoes, cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the mango slices and simmer until soft.
Mash a few mango slices against the side of the pot to release their sourness into the broth.
Add the radish and simmer until it starts to turn translucent.
Add the eggplant and okra and simmer until tender.
Add the chilies and season with fish sauce. Taste for sourness.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve hot.

tips: Pick the hardest, most sour mangoes you can find, like the green carabao mangoes sold for eating with bagoong.

title: Sinigang na baboy sa batuan
intro: A Visayan-style pork sinigang soured with batuan, a small round fruit that gives a deep, rounded sourness, with lemongrass for fragrance.

items.name: stalks lemongrass (tanglad)
items.note: bruised and tied in a knot

steps.text: Bring the pork and water to a boil and skim off the foam.
Add the onion, tomatoes and lemongrass, cover and simmer until the pork is nearly tender.
Add the batuan and simmer until they are very soft.
Scoop out the batuan, mash them through a strainer back into the pot and discard the seeds and skins. Remove the lemongrass.
Add the okra, eggplant and long beans and simmer until tender.
Add the chilies and season with fish sauce.
Turn off the heat, add the sweet potato leaves if using and cover until wilted. Serve hot.

tips: Batuan is sold fresh in Visayan markets and frozen or dried elsewhere. If using dried batuan, use 6 to 8 pieces and simmer them a little longer.

title: Sinigang na baboy sa pinya
intro: Pork sinigang with chunks of fresh pineapple, which add a fruity sweetness and their own tang to the tamarind broth.

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Bring the pork and water to a boil and skim off the foam.
Add the onion and tomatoes, cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the pineapple and radish and simmer until the radish turns translucent.
Add the long beans and simmer until tender.
Stir in the tamarind soup base a little at a time until the broth is sour with a fruity finish. Add the chilies and season with fish sauce.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve hot.

tips: Fresh pineapple is sourer than canned. If you only have canned chunks, drain them well and add a little extra tamarind.

title: Sinigang na pata
intro: Pork hock simmered slowly until the skin turns soft and sticky and the broth turns rich, then soured with fresh tamarind. Hearty sinigang for a long weekend lunch.

steps.text: Put the pork hock in a large pot, cover with water and boil for 5 minutes. Drain, rinse the pieces and wash the pot.
Return the pork to the pot with the 2.5 liters of water, the onion and tomatoes. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer over low heat until the skin is soft and the meat pulls from the bone.
While the broth simmers, boil the tamarind in the 2 cups of water until the skins split and the flesh turns soft.
Mash the tamarind in its water with a fork, then press it through a strainer into a bowl. Discard the seeds and skins and keep the thick sour juice.
Add the taro and simmer until soft.
Add the radish and long beans and simmer until tender.
Stir in the tamarind juice to taste, then add the chilies and season with fish sauce.
Turn off the heat, add the bok choy and cover until it wilts. Serve hot.

tips: The quick first boil cleans the hock and gives a clearer broth. A pressure cooker cuts the long simmer to about 40 minutes.

title: Sinigang na lechon
intro: Leftover roast pork simmered in tamarind broth, so the skin softens and the smoky, salty meat flavors the whole pot. The usual way to finish a lechon after a party.

items.name: leftover lechon or lechon kawali
items.note: chopped into serving pieces, with skin

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Put the lechon, water, onion and tomatoes in a pot and bring to a boil. Lower the heat and simmer until the skin softens and the broth turns savory.
Meanwhile, boil the tamarind in the 2 cups of water until the skins split and the flesh turns soft.
Mash the tamarind in its water with a fork, then press it through a strainer into a bowl. Discard the seeds and skins and keep the thick sour juice.
Add the radish and simmer until it starts to turn translucent.
Add the eggplant and long beans and simmer until tender.
Stir in the tamarind juice to taste and add the chilies. Season with fish sauce only after tasting, since the lechon is already salty.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve hot.

tips: Leftover lechon sauce or liver sauce does not belong here: it makes the broth sweet and cloudy. Keep it for the side.

title: Sinigang na baka
intro: Beef short ribs simmered until fork-tender in a tamarind broth with taro, radish and long beans. Beefier and richer than pork sinigang, with the same sharp sourness.

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Bring the beef and water to a boil in a large pot and skim off the foam.
Add the onion and tomatoes, cover and simmer over low heat until the beef is tender. Add hot water if the level drops below the meat.
While the broth simmers, boil the tamarind in the 2 cups of water until the skins split and the flesh turns soft.
Mash the tamarind in its water with a fork, then press it through a strainer into a bowl. Discard the seeds and skins and keep the thick sour juice.
Add the taro and simmer until soft.
Add the radish and long beans and simmer until tender.
Stir in the tamarind juice to taste, add the chilies and season with fish sauce.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve hot.

tips: A pressure cooker gets the short ribs tender in about 45 minutes. Skim the fat off the top before adding the vegetables for a cleaner broth.

title: Sinigang na kenchi
intro: Beef shank with its tendons, or kenchi, simmered for hours until the tendons turn soft and gelatinous, then soured with tamarind. A rich, sticky sinigang for beef lovers.

steps.text: Bring the beef and water to a boil in a large pot and skim off the foam.
Add the onion and tomatoes, cover and simmer over low heat until the tendons are soft and the meat is tender. Top up with hot water as needed.
While the broth simmers, boil the tamarind in the 2 cups of water until the skins split and the flesh turns soft.
Mash the tamarind in its water with a fork, then press it through a strainer into a bowl. Discard the seeds and skins and keep the thick sour juice.
Add the radish and simmer until it starts to turn translucent.
Add the eggplant, okra and long beans and simmer until tender.
Stir in the tamarind juice to taste, add the chilies and season with fish sauce.
Turn off the heat, add the bok choy and cover until it wilts. Serve hot.

tips: Kenchi needs time. If the tendons are still chewy, keep simmering: they go from rubbery to soft quite suddenly. A pressure cooker takes about 1 hour.

title: Kansi
intro: An Ilonggo beef shank soup with bone marrow, soured with batuan and cooked with unripe jackfruit and lemongrass. Golden from annatto, rich, sour and a little spicy.

items.name: stalks lemongrass (tanglad)
items.note: bruised and tied in a knot

steps.text: Bring the beef and water to a boil in a large pot and skim off the foam.
Add the lemongrass, onion and garlic. Cover and simmer over low heat until the meat is very tender and pulls from the bone.
Add the batuan and simmer until soft.
Scoop out the batuan, mash them through a strainer back into the pot and discard the seeds and skins. Remove the lemongrass.
Soak the annatto seeds in the hot water, rubbing them between your fingers until the water turns deep orange.
Add the jackfruit to the pot and simmer until tender.
Strain the annatto water into the soup and discard the seeds. Add the chilies and season with fish sauce, salt and pepper.
Simmer a few minutes more to bring the flavors together. Serve hot, with a piece of marrow bone in each bowl.

tips: Wear gloves or oil your hands and knife when cutting fresh jackfruit: its sap is very sticky. Frozen cut jackfruit works too.

title: Sinigang na corned beef
intro: Canned corned beef sauteed with garlic and tomatoes, then simmered in tamarind broth with radish and water spinach. A quick, salty-sour pantry sinigang for busy days.

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat. Saute the garlic until fragrant, then the onion and tomatoes until the tomatoes soften.
Add the corned beef and stir, breaking it up, until it is heated through and lightly browned.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil.
Add the radish and simmer until it starts to turn translucent.
Add the long beans and simmer until tender.
Stir in the tamarind soup base and add the chili. Taste before adding any fish sauce, since corned beef is salty.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve right away.

tips: Leaner corned beef gives a cleaner broth. If yours is very fatty, skim some fat off the top before adding the vegetables.

title: Sinampalukang manok
intro: Chicken sauteed with plenty of ginger, then simmered with young tamarind pods and tender tamarind leaves. Gingery, gently sour and brothy, with a fresh, leafy tang.

items.name: ginger
items.note: peeled and cut into thin strips

items.name: young green tamarind pods
items.note: or 1 pack (22 g) tamarind soup base

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat. Saute the ginger until fragrant, then the garlic, onion and tomatoes until soft.
Add the chicken and stir until it turns opaque on all sides. Add the fish sauce, cover and let the chicken sweat in its own juices.
Pour in the water and add the tamarind pods. Bring to a boil, then simmer, covered, until the chicken is cooked and the pods are soft.
Lift out the tamarind pods, mash them in a strainer with a ladle of broth and press the juice back into the pot. Discard the skins and seeds.
Add the chilies and taste. Add more fish sauce or more mashed tamarind until the broth is savory and pleasantly sour.
Add the tamarind leaves and simmer briefly until they wilt and turn olive green.
Serve hot with rice.

tips: Young tamarind leaves are sold by the bundle in wet markets. If you cannot find them, the dish still works with just the pods and a handful of chili leaves.

title: Sinigang na manok
intro: Chicken pieces sauteed with onion and tomato, then simmered in tamarind broth with radish, okra and long beans. Lighter and quicker than pork sinigang.

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat and saute the onion and tomatoes until soft.
Add the chicken and 1 tablespoon of the fish sauce and stir until the chicken turns opaque.
Pour in the water, bring to a boil and skim off any foam. Cover and simmer until the chicken is cooked through.
While the broth simmers, boil the tamarind in the 2 cups of water until the skins split and the flesh turns soft.
Mash the tamarind in its water with a fork, then press it through a strainer into a bowl. Discard the seeds and skins and keep the thick sour juice.
Add the radish and simmer until it starts to turn translucent.
Add the okra and long beans and simmer until tender.
Stir in the tamarind juice to taste, add the chilies and season with the remaining fish sauce.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve hot.

tips: Thighs and drumsticks stay juicier than breast. If you use breast, add it 10 minutes later.

title: Sinigang na gulay
intro: A meatless sinigang packed with vegetables and fried tofu, soured with fresh tamarind and seasoned with salt instead of fish sauce. Bright, sour and filling.

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium-high heat and fry the tofu, turning, until golden on all sides. Drain on paper towels.
Put the water, onion, tomatoes and taro in a pot. Bring to a boil, then simmer until the taro is soft and the tomatoes have broken down.
Meanwhile, boil the tamarind in the 2 cups of water until the skins split and the flesh turns soft.
Mash the tamarind in its water with a fork, then press it through a strainer into a bowl. Discard the seeds and skins and keep the thick sour juice.
Add the radish and simmer until it starts to turn translucent.
Add the eggplant, okra and long beans and simmer until tender.
Stir in the tamarind juice to taste, then the salt and chilies. Add the fried tofu and simmer just to heat through.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve hot.

tips: Mash one or two pieces of the cooked taro into the broth to give it more body, which makes up for the missing meat.

title: Sinigang na hipon
intro: Head-on shrimp cooked briefly in a sharp tamarind broth with radish, okra, long beans and water spinach. Quick, sweet from the shrimp and very sour.

items.name: rice wash or water
items.note: rice wash is the water from the second rinse of rice

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Bring the rice wash, onion and tomatoes to a boil in a pot, then simmer until the tomatoes soften.
Meanwhile, boil the tamarind in the 2 cups of water until the skins split and the flesh turns soft.
Mash the tamarind in its water with a fork, then press it through a strainer into a bowl. Discard the seeds and skins and keep the thick sour juice.
Add the radish to the pot and simmer until it starts to turn translucent.
Add the okra and long beans and simmer until tender.
Stir in the tamarind juice to taste, add the chilies and season with fish sauce.
Add the shrimp and simmer just until they turn pink and curl.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve right away.

tips: Press a few shrimp heads against the side of the pot with a ladle to release the fat into the broth. Do not let the shrimp boil long or they turn tough.

title: Sinigang na hipon sa bayabas
intro: Shrimp in a fragrant, mildly sour broth made from ripe guavas, with taro to give it body. Sweeter and softer than tamarind sinigang.

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Put the water, onion, tomatoes, guavas and taro in a pot. Bring to a boil, then simmer until the guavas and taro are very soft.
Scoop out the guavas and mash them through a strainer back into the pot. Discard the seeds and skins.
Add the long beans and simmer until tender.
Add the chilies and season with fish sauce.
Add the shrimp and simmer just until they turn pink.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve right away.

tips: If the guavas are very ripe and the broth tastes more sweet than sour, add a few kamias or a squeeze of calamansi.

title: Sinigang na hipon sa kamias
intro: Shrimp in a clear, tart broth soured with fresh kamias, with eggplant, long beans and bok choy. Light, sharp and quick to cook.

steps.text: Bring the water, onion and tomatoes to a boil and simmer until the tomatoes soften.
Add the kamias and simmer until they turn olive green and soft. Press some against the side of the pot to release their juice.
Add the eggplant and long beans and simmer until tender.
Add the chilies and season with fish sauce.
Add the shrimp and simmer just until they turn pink.
Turn off the heat, add the bok choy and cover until it wilts. Serve right away.

tips: Taste the broth before adding the shrimp: if it needs more sourness, simmer a few more kamias first.

title: Sinigang na hipon sa mangga
intro: Shrimp simmered in a broth soured with green mango, which gives it a fresh, tangy sourness and a light fruity aroma.

items.name: large green (unripe) mango
items.note: peeled and sliced off the seed

items.name: bunch water spinach (kangkong)
items.note: leaves and tender stems, about 200 g

steps.text: Bring the water, onion, tomatoes and mango to a boil, then simmer until the mango is soft.
Mash a few mango slices against the side of the pot to release their sourness.
Add the radish and simmer until it starts to turn translucent.
Add the okra and long beans and simmer until tender.
Add the chilies and season with fish sauce.
Add the shrimp and simmer just until they turn pink.
Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and cover until wilted. Serve right away.

tips: Use the sourest, hardest mango you can find. A mango that has started to turn yellow makes the broth too sweet.

title: Sinigang na hipon sa calamansi
intro: Shrimp in a light ginger and tomato broth soured at the end with fresh calamansi juice. Bright, citrusy and quick, with a cleaner sourness than tamarind.

steps.text: Bring the water, onion, tomatoes and ginger to a boil, then simmer until the tomatoes soften.
Add the radish and simmer until it starts to turn translucent.
Add the long beans and simmer until tender.
Add the chilies and season with fish sauce.
Add the shrimp and simmer just until they turn pink.
Turn off the heat. Add the bok choy, then stir in the calamansi juice a little at a time until the broth is as sour as you like.
Cover for a minute to wilt the greens and serve right away.

tips: Add the calamansi juice off the heat: boiled calamansi turns bitter. Squeeze the fruit gently and leave out the seeds for the same reason.
